courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
md: Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
md: Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
md: Parler's public posts were meant to be readable one at a time. Sequential ids plus no rate limit turned "anyone can read a post" into "anyone can copy the entire site, with GPS locations". Authorization decides who may read an object; rate limits and unpredictable ids decide how cheaply someone can read all of them. You need both.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: A domain is not a wall. Domains in one forest trust each other automatically, and the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root is an administrator in every domain (next lesson). Plan protection for the whole forest, not one domain at a time.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AS-REP roasting and password spraying against AD
md: Turning off pre-authentication hands out crackable material to anyone; 4768 with pre-auth type 0 finds it. Spraying hides under per-account lockout; count distinct accounts per source in 4771 and 4776, not failures per account.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Tiering fails quietly through agents. A backup, monitoring or patching tool that runs as SYSTEM on DCs, managed from a Tier 1 console, makes that console Tier 0. List everything installed on DCs and everyone who controls it.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: PDF: objects, filters, automatic actions and JavaScript
md: Do not open a suspicious PDF in your everyday reader to 'see what it says'. Readers run JavaScript and follow actions; that is the point of the file. Triage with pdfid and parse with pdf-parser, which only read bytes.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
md: Crypto flaws in ransomware are rare, and once published they can be fixed in the next version. Plan recovery around offline backups; treat a decryptor as a lucky bonus, and get one only from a trusted source.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: What this means for engineers: safe languages, fuzzing, defaults
md: Prevent, then detect, then mitigate. Memory-safe languages remove bug classes; sanitizers and fuzzing catch what remains; mitigations on by default raise the cost of what slips through; and fast patching shortens the window. Every rung an attacker must climb is one you can remove.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Scoring outcomes and measuring detection coverage
md: Averages hide shapes. An average score of 3 can be every technique alerting but never triaged, or half the techniques perfect and half invisible. Always report the distribution and the gap categories with the average, and never report coverage as "techniques with a rule tagged".

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
md: The paper calls r = 1 necessary but not sufficient: an agent that issues the correct return *without* asking for confirmation still scores 1, even though it broke policy. Database comparison catches wrong outcomes, not bad conduct along the way.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Permissions, traces and evaluation
md: Permission checks are only as strong as the sandbox behind them. Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments for agents; run untrusted or autonomous agents in a container or VM with limited network and credentials, and reserve modes that skip approval for those isolated environments.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Misconception: if the agent ran the tests itself and reported success, the work is verified. The report is model output, and tests the agent wrote or could edit are not independent. Run the checks in the harness, on a clean copy, with tests the agent did not control.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: How an LLM app is built: one stream of tokens
md: An LLM app has one channel. Instructions and data are both tokens in the context window, and the model, not your code, decides what each token means.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Approval gates and egress allowlists
md: Gate side effects with a real, informed human decision. Constrain network egress to exact hosts in code the model cannot influence. Together they turn "the model was fooled" into "the model asked and was refused".

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Defence in layers: privilege separation, provenance and egress
md: Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do harm: it cannot reach what it should not read, cannot act without a check it cannot talk past, and cannot send data anywhere you did not list.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Why AI text needs a planted signal
md: A text watermark is a keyed, pseudorandom preference applied at sampling time. Detection re-derives the preference from the text and asks whether the text agrees with it far more often than chance.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks on text watermarks: edits, paraphrase, spoofing and stealing
md: Text watermarks fail in four ways: edits that re-randomize the seeds, meaning-preserving rewrites, spoofing that plants the signal in text the provider never wrote, and stealing by learning the pattern. Treat a positive detection as statistical evidence about origin, not proof of authorship, and a negative one as no information.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: A score is only as good as its model of normal. Mean and standard deviation break under masking; median and MAD fix that for one variable. For data with clusters and local structure you need scores that look at the joint shape of the data, which is what the next lessons build.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Under heavy imbalance, judge detectors by ranking quality where you will act: AP and the PR curve for the whole ranking, precision@k for the review budget. ROC-AUC hides false alarms because it divides them by the huge number of normal points.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
md: The code travels through the browser, so assume it can leak. PKCE ties redeeming it to a secret that never left the client that started the flow.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Classic JWT bugs: alg none, RS256 to HS256, kid and jku
md: Every one of these bugs is the same mistake: letting data inside the unverified token decide how the token is verified. The receiver fixes the algorithm, the key set and the audience; the token only gets to say which of the receiver's keys it used.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Design review in the cycle: deciding which changes get a threat model
md: A design review that happens after the code is written is an audit, not a design review. If the triage questionnaire lives in the pull request template instead of the design template, the expensive decisions (which vendor, where the data lives) are already made.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Security champions, bug bounties and disclosure programmes
md: Champions scale security inside; a VDP with safe harbour invites help from outside. Both fail without the basics: someone answers the reports, and fixes have owners and deadlines.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
md: Steal creates the need for **undo**, no-force creates the need for **redo**. ARIES allows both, so it must do both, using only the log and a little state stored on each page.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on
md: All four designs encode the same idea: one shared vector space, two roles. Use the exact pair (prefixes, instructions or input types) that the model was trained with, on the side it was trained for.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
md: Order of checks for each call: cache first (free, instant), then dedupe in-flight duplicates, then a concurrency limit and a rate limiter, then the API with bounded jittered retries. Anything that is not latency-sensitive goes to a batch job. Every side effect is keyed so that re-running the job is safe.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS turns "read, compute, write" into "read, compute, write *only if what I read is still there*". The retry loop is the general recipe: load, compute from the loaded value, CAS, and on failure recompute from the value CAS returned.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with CLAP audio and text embeddings
md: Choosing an approach: use a pretrained tagger's scores directly when AudioSet classes cover your needs; train a small head on frozen embeddings when you have a few hundred labeled clips; fine-tune when you have more data and compute; use CLAP-style zero-shot when labels change often or you have no labeled audio, and expect lower accuracy than a supervised head on the same classes.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Online attacks: brute force, credential stuffing, password spraying
md: Brute force is one account, many passwords. Credential stuffing is many leaked pairs. Spraying is one password, many accounts. MFA and breached-password checks defeat all three; detection needs counts across accounts, not just per account.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval
md: A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Set `max_tokens` close to the longest answer you really need. The AWS docs say it directly: if you hit TPM quotas earlier than expected, reduce max_tokens to better approximate your completions. Measure real output lengths from the `OutputTokenCount` metric that Bedrock publishes to CloudWatch, the AWS monitoring service.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Firmware images: layout, signatures and entropy
md: Everything here uses an image we built from our own code. Real vendor firmware is often covered by licence terms, and some contains other parties' secrets; analyse only devices and images you own or are authorised to test, and never download firmware to attack devices you do not control.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Does ternary scale? The evidence and its limits
md: Read the scale. The accuracy evidence in the b1.58 paper stops at 3.9B parameters and 100B tokens, plus one 3B model at 2T tokens. Everything larger is a measurement of speed, memory and energy, not of quality.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: Predictors learn *regularity*: biased branches, periodic patterns, and (next lesson) correlations with other branches. A branch on random data with a 50/50 split is mispredicted about half the time on every CPU, no matter how clever the predictor.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: IPC and Mojo: the renderer asks, the browser decides
md: Ask of every IPC method: which argument identifies *who is asking*, and does the privileged side get that from its own state or from the message? Identity must come from the browser's state. Everything in the message is attacker input to be range-checked, type-checked and allowlisted.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Who finds browser bugs: bounties, in-the-wild 0-days and practice
md: Across every case in this course the pattern is the same: one bug class (type confusion, use-after-free, a stale check, a trusted value from a less privileged process), one boundary it crossed, and one fix that either corrects the logic or moves the boundary. Defenders win the n-day race by knowing which of their products sit behind which boundary.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: No engine minimizes read, write and space amplification at once. B+trees pay on random writes. Leveled LSMs pay in rewrites. Tiered LSMs pay in reads and temporary space. Pick the cost your workload can afford, then tune T, Bloom bits and compaction bandwidth.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
md: Do not let IT set the MTD by asking "how fast could we restore it?". That gives you the current capability, not the requirement. The BIA asks the process owner "how long until this becomes unacceptable?", and the gap between the two answers is the work of the rest of this course.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
md: Granularity is a recovery requirement. In multi-tenant systems (one data store, many customers), "restore the database" also rolls back every unaffected customer. Write RTOs per restore size (one record, one tenant, many tenants, everything) and test each, because they are different procedures with very different times.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
md: Do not let the recovery team be the crisis team. Engineers in the middle of a restore should not also be negotiating with customers and drafting press statements; and executives should not be choosing which database snapshot to restore. Separate the roles, connect them with a fixed reporting rhythm.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Build it: a byte GPT, then a two-level patch model
md: A byte GPT is a GPT with a 256-entry vocabulary; the cost is more positions per byte. A two-level model fixes that by running the big network once per patch, and stays causal only through two shifts: one patch for the global input, one byte for the local input.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: Tools such as AddressSanitizer and **fuzzing** (feeding the program huge numbers of automatically generated or mutated inputs and watching for crashes) find many of these bugs, but only on inputs that actually run. The Android team describes them as treating symptoms rather than the root cause, and notes that coverage stays low without constant pressure on teams to fuzz and triage.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
md: Recipe for an unsafe-backed type: write the invariants down, keep the fields they mention private, make every unsafe block's SAFETY comment cite one invariant, and run tests that hit the edges (empty, first grow, full, drop with live elements) under Miri.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Capacity is set by size, conflicts by associativity and address bits. A bigger cache fixes capacity misses; more ways or a less regular stride fixes conflict misses; nothing but prefetching (loading lines before the program asks for them, lesson 4) hides cold misses.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
md: "It comes from our own API" is not the same as "trusted". The value was typed by some user before your API stored it. React's own Markdown example is safe only because the rendered HTML is shown back to the same user who wrote it, and because the team trusts the Markdown parser to have no bugs.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
md: Misconception: "ATT&CK IDs are permanent". MITRE reorganises the matrix: Disable or Modify Cloud Log moved from T1562.008 to T1685.002, and tactics have been renamed. Map rules to IDs, but review the mapping when a new ATT&CK version ships.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
md: Design as if any one credential will be stolen tomorrow. The test of an architecture is not "can an attacker get in?" but "what can one stolen login destroy or read?" Keep the data and its last good copy behind different identities, in different accounts.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Azure in depth: role assignments, Run Command and PIM
md: In Azure, the keys to escalation are writing role assignments and running code where a privileged identity lives. Make powerful roles eligible through PIM, delegate assignments with conditions instead of Owner, and treat Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM as equal to that VM's managed identity.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
md: Prefer roles and temporary credentials everywhere. AWS's own best practices say to require human users to use federation with temporary credentials and to require workloads to use IAM roles. Long-term access keys are for the few cases nothing else supports, and they need rotation, monitoring and the narrowest possible permissions.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Scaling is a modelling choice, not a cleanup step. Standardising says "one standard deviation of every feature counts the same", which silently gives a noisy, unimportant feature as much say as a crucial one. Decide how much each feature should weigh, then scale to match. k-means, DBSCAN's eps and every method in this course measure distance, and none of them is scale free.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: The optimizer assumes the program has no UB: signed overflow never happens, differently typed pointers never alias, dereferenced pointers are not null. Code that breaks those rules can change behavior at -O2. Find it with sanitizers and the -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switches, then fix the code.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission
md: Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
md: Misconception: "filler tokens did not help, so all of a model's reasoning must be in the words." Lanham's result shows that particular models did not learn to use filler. Pfau et al. show training can teach a transformer to compute across meaningless tokens on suitable problems, and nothing in a monitor's view of "......" would reveal what was computed.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: These methods sit uneasily with "keep optimization pressure off the CoT". VFT trains directly on CoT content. The difference from Baker et al.'s failure is direction and timing: it rewards saying more, before RL, and the RL reward never reads the CoT. VFT was tested on one 8B model with multiple-choice cues; whether it holds for frontier agents is open.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The LLM engine loop: hiding CPU scheduling behind the GPU
md: An engine step is a two-stage pipeline: CPU work and GPU work. Overlap turns the period from their sum into their maximum, CUDA graphs shrink the launch cost inside the GPU stage, and the CPU must never become the larger stage. The price of planning ahead is seeing each token one step late.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
md: Reranker latency is about k divided by throughput. You control it with three knobs: how many candidates you rerank, how large the model is, and how many pairs you can run in parallel. Each trades against accuracy or cost.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: MACs and HMAC: integrity with a shared key
md: Never build a MAC from hash(key + message), and never compare secrets with ==. Use HMAC (or an AEAD, which includes a MAC) and hmac.compare_digest.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
md: "We patched the oracle" is weaker than "we removed RSA key exchange". ROBOT found new oracles in implementations that already had Bleichenbacher countermeasures, because a single timing or TCP behaviour difference is enough.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Downgrade and protocol confusion: one key, one purpose
md: Security is set by the weakest place a key is accepted and the weakest option a negotiation allows. Give each key one job in one protocol, put the job's name inside everything it signs, and remove options rather than defending them.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: A Hopper CUTLASS mainloop is a ring of shared memory stages: a producer warp keeps TMA loads ahead, consumer warpgroups run wgmma on full stages, and full and empty barriers pass ownership of each stage back and forth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Treat CXL memory as a far NUMA node: same instructions, same caching, about 70 to 100 ns more per miss for a nearby device, bandwidth comparable to a DDR channel per x8 link. Whether it is a win depends on how many misses you send there.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
md: After Van Buren: 'without authorization' asks whether you may enter the system at all; 'exceeds authorized access' asks whether you entered an area your access does not extend to. Motive is not the test. DOJ policy adds: decline good-faith research, and do not charge contract-only theories.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
md: The exemption itself says it is "not a safe harbor from, or defense to" other laws, naming the CFAA. Circumventing a TPM on someone else's server can be legal under 1201 and still be unauthorised access. And the exemption covers the act of circumvention, not distributing circumvention tools.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
md: "The IRB said it was not human research" and "no bug was merged" did not end the matter. Ethics review is a floor, like law. If your study manipulates people's behaviour, they are participants, whatever the form says.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Domain weights are not a zero-sum allocation of quality. Because very easy and very noisy domains need few samples, and domains transfer to each other, a better mixture can lower loss on **every** domain at once, including the ones it shrinks.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
md: Think in two levels. **Within** a domain, clean and filter documents (lesson 9's rules and deduplication, then a classifier). **Across** domains, choose weights with a method like DoReMi or a fitted mixing model. Then rerun the mixing step, because filtering changes each domain's size and difficulty.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Seeing security from the data's side: copies, states and stages
md: Start every data security question from the data: what is it, where are *all* its copies (including tickets, exports and backups), who can read each one, how can it leave, and when will each copy be destroyed.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security I: accounts, grants, views and the revoke trap
md: Separate owner, application, analyst and admin roles; grant explicit columns or views rather than whole tables; never rely on revoking one column from a table-level grant; and keep grants in version control so drift is visible.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: An alarm nobody should trip: why deception detects
md: A decoy has no legitimate users, so the number of things that touch it is tiny. That, not cleverness, is where its signal comes from. Every design choice in this course protects that property.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Deception in Active Directory: honey accounts and honey SPNs
md: Your own tools will touch decoys: vulnerability scanners, identity-governance jobs that read every account, auditors' scripts, and secret scanners that verify the keys they find (TruffleHog's check calls sts:GetCallerIdentity, which fires a decoy AWS key). List them before go-live and route their hits to a review queue, not to silence. A decoy that a weekly script trips is a decoy everyone learns to ignore.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
md: Determinism leaks are easy to write. Reading the real clock, spawning an OS thread, seeding from OS entropy, or iterating a hash map whose order is randomized per process (Rust's default `HashMap` is) all make the same seed produce different runs. FoundationDB avoids multithreaded concurrency entirely and deploys one node per core instead.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Caches and artifacts: how Ultralytics was poisoned
md: Anything a privileged job reads (a cache, an artifact, a downloaded tool, a config file) is part of its input. Ask who could have written it. If the answer includes a fork, a PR or a comment, the privileged job must treat it as untrusted data or not read it at all.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
md: The first attempt kept the GPT's learned position table (wpe). The diffusion model stalled: after 5,000 steps its bound was 2.94 nats per character against the GPT's 1.52. Swapping in rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which LLaDA uses, fixed it: with RoPE the bound reached 1.96 after only 3,000 steps.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput is not throughput. A colocated GPU at 4 req/s still produces plenty of tokens per second, but in the toy run only 28% of requests meet both SLOs. If you only tracked throughput, that overloaded point would look like the best one.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Chunked prefill bounds interference inside one GPU; disaggregation removes it and lets each phase get its own hardware, parallelism and scale. Pick by measuring per-GPU goodput under your SLOs, prompt lengths and interconnect, not by architecture preference.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The registry in depth, and proving a USB drive was used
md: A VSN changes when a volume is reformatted and is only 32 bits on FAT, so a match is strong corroboration, not a unique fingerprint. Combine it with the device serial and times. The meanings of the 0x64 to 0x67 properties also vary by Windows build: test on a reference system before testifying to them.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
md: A common misreading: larger alpha prunes *more*. It is the opposite. The removal test gets harder to pass as alpha grows, so more candidates survive, the average degree rises (up to the cap R), and search paths get shorter. The cost is memory and more distance computations per hop.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: KTO keeps DPO's implicit reward and reference model but drops pairing: each example is scored against a shared reference point (the estimated KL drift) instead of against a sibling answer. That lets it train on binary feedback, and on imbalanced data via $\lambda_D, \lambda_U$.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Scientist is for code that only reads. Its README says that because the candidate may or may not run, it is only safe for wrapping methods that do not change data. Write paths need different checks, such as comparing stored rows after the fact.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: X3DH step by step: four Diffie-Hellman results, one key
md: X3DH gets authentication from DH (identity keys appear in DH1 and DH2) and forward secrecy from keys that are deleted (EK, OPK, and SPK once it is rotated out). The prekey signature exists for a narrower reason, covered next.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Key transparency: from CONIKS to WhatsApp and iMessage
md: Key transparency turns "trust the server's answer" into "the server must commit publicly to its answer". Inclusion proofs show a key is in the log; consistency checks, self-monitoring and auditors make sure there is only one log.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Telegram's MTProto, and why messengers need proofs
md: Common misconception: "Telegram is encrypted, so it is like Signal". By default it is client-to-server encryption, like TLS to a web service: the provider can read cloud chats and all groups. Only optional one-to-one secret chats are end to end.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Common misconception: "eBPF is safe, so tracing can't hurt production." The verifier guarantees the kernel won't crash or hang, but it does not bound *how often* your program runs. A kprobe on a function called millions of times per second can still cost a large fraction of every CPU.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Why appliances are hard to defend: patches, logs and trust
md: Treat an appliance as a server you cannot see into. Get its logs out as they are written, limit the secrets it holds, and plan in advance for the day you must rebuild it.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Detecting a compromised appliance from the outside
md: When you cannot see inside a device, watch its edges: every connection it starts, every session that changes address, every account that uses it, and every configuration change. Those records live on other systems the intruder does not control.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
md: A length term changes which correct answers GRPO reinforces most. Without it, all correct answers in a group are equal; with it, the shortest correct one gets the largest advantage.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing
md: Deciding whether to think is often a bigger lever than shortening the thinking. Evaluate every option, from NoThinking to full thinking, on an accuracy-versus-tokens frontier per difficulty level, and check whether accuracy differences exceed the noise of your test set.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Case mapping and case folding: when lower() is not one-to-one
md: Locale-aware case mapping makes it worse: in Turkish, `I` lower-cases to dotless ı. Code that lower-cases with the server's locale can give different answers on different machines. For identifiers, use locale-independent case folding, as Python's `str.casefold()` is.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Polyglot files, content sniffing and LangSec
md: Checking the first bytes of an upload is not validation. A file can carry one format's signature and another format's content. If a file must be an image, decode it with an image library and re-encode it to a fresh file; whatever was hidden in it does not survive.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
md: Microsoft states AppLocker is "a defense-in-depth security feature and not considered a defensible Windows security feature": it does not meet Microsoft's servicing criteria, so a bypass is not treated as a vulnerability. Use it to raise the bar and to control what users run; use App Control for Business where you need a security boundary.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
md: Event-based methods need step changes. Hart's own NALM page lists three appliance classes: ON/OFF (bulbs, toasters), multi-state (washing machines, dishwashers with fill, rinse and spin states) and continuously variable (light dimmers, variable-speed tools). The last class is hard to monitor nonintrusively because it does not generate step changes in power.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: The independence assumption double-counts correlated fields. Company name and website domain usually agree or disagree together, so adding both full weights overstates the evidence. Merge strongly correlated fields into one comparison, or check calibration on labeled pairs: whether pairs scored 0.9 really match about 90% of the time.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: Count who can become Global Administrator, not only who is one: role assigners, admin credential resetters, app credential managers and hybrid identity admins. Keep the count small, make it eligible rather than active, and keep two tested emergency accounts outside it.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Entra access is a chain: a 60 to 90 minute access token renewed by a 90-day refresh token that is bound to user and client, not to a resource. Revocation cuts the chain; CAE cuts the current link at Exchange, SharePoint, Teams and Graph.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: A Conditional Access policy set is only as strong as what it does not cover. Inventory the exclusions, the service principals and the allowed flows, block legacy authentication and device code, and test every change in report-only mode first.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
md: Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: Common misconception: "the binary has every mitigation enabled, so this overflow is not a security issue." Every mitigation in this course has a known bypass class (lesson 14), and real exploits combine several bugs to get past them. An overflow is a security bug whether or not today's exploit techniques reach it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer (a race detector such as ThreadSanitizer, which flags conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory) to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt
md: Compression is lossy, and lossy is only safe when it is **unbiased**. Probabilistic quantization and scaled subsampling are unbiased per client, so their errors average out across a round. A biased compressor (rounding to nearest, keeping only the largest entries) pushes every client the same way, which looks like drift in disguise.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
md: Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Build it: a DeepSeekMoE layer with bias balancing in your GPT
md: Do not read quality conclusions off a run this small. Character-level Shakespeare with a 3.65M-parameter MoE (0.9M active) trains in under an hour per run on a CPU; differences of a few thousandths in validation loss between configurations are within seed noise. What this lab shows reliably is the mechanism: what the router does without balancing, and how each method changes the expert loads.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Case: Baton Drop and BlackLotus, a signed door left open
md: "Fixed" and "no longer trusted" are different states. Until the vulnerable signed binary is revoked or rolled past, the fix protects only machines whose attacker politely uses the new file.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-2 kernel tile by tile: forward, backward, parallelism
md: Every later kernel is this loop. FlashAttention-3's producer warps load $K_j, V_j$ and its pipeline overlaps the next $S_{ij}$ with the current $PV$; FlashAttention-4 moves $S$ and $P$ out of registers into a new on-chip memory, pairs thread blocks for the five backward matmuls, and orders causal tiles longest first (lessons 6 to 8). Only the mapping onto hardware changes.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: The paper's design in one line: one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
md: Testing samples behaviors; verification covers all of them. Model checking covers every behavior of a bounded model of the design. Proof covers every behavior of the code, but only for the properties you wrote down.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus on real data: views, quantifiers, triggers and failed proofs
md: A failing assert does not mean the fact is false. With quantifiers it often means no trigger fired. Before weakening the spec, check whether the needed term ever appears in the proof.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: Do not copy FP16's overflow handling. FP16 automatic mixed precision (PyTorch's autocast with a dynamic loss scaler) skips the update and shrinks the loss scale when an overflow appears. The FP8 paper explains that overflows are much more likely in FP8's narrow range, so skipping would discard too many steps; FP8 recipes **saturate** out-of-range values to the maximum instead.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust and safety: what these teams defend
md: Fraud and abuse use features that work. You cannot patch them away; you make them expensive for attackers and cheap for honest users, and you measure both.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviour and velocity: counting what happens over time
md: Velocity turns weak single events into strong patterns. Store counts in time buckets per key, combine them with outcomes (declines, failures), and expect honest edge cases at every threshold.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: EMV chips, the 2015 liability shift, and fraud moving online
md: A chip makes each transaction's data single use, so copying it is worthless. The 2015 US liability shift used fraud costs to force adoption, and fraud moved to the channel still using static data: card-not-present.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake reviews and content abuse
md: Never build your own collection of illegal material to test a detector. Work with the hash lists, tools and legal reporting channels that exist for this purpose, and route matches to trained staff under your legal team's procedures.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Group commit: one WAL flush makes many transactions durable
md: Group commit does not make any single commit faster. With one client there is nothing to share and latency is one full flush. It raises **throughput** when many sessions commit concurrently, and it keeps latency from exploding as they queue.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Seeds, dictionaries and corpus minimisation
md: A good campaign starts with small valid seeds per feature, a dictionary of the format's tokens, and a minimised corpus that you keep and reuse. When coverage plateaus, improve the inputs and harness rather than adding CPU time.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Variant analysis and patch diffing: one bug, many siblings
md: When you fix a bug, write its pattern down and search for it before closing the ticket. Shellshock needed six CVEs because the first fix addressed one symptom of a design problem; variant analysis and fuzzing the patched code found the rest.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
md: Both indexes trade exactness of the first step for speed: a trigram index proposes candidates by a cheap overlap count, a BK-tree rules out subtrees with the triangle inequality. Neither changes the final score; you still verify candidates with the metric you trust.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
md: Retrieval is cheap and noisy; verification is strict. Each match is a full alignment that predicts many other stars, and the Bayes factor multiplies independent evidence, so a true match passes 1e9 within a handful of stars while chance matches almost never do.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Pixels in memory: NHWC, NCHW, pitch and a warp's 96 bytes
md: For a per-pixel operator, layout plus pitch decides how wide an aligned access each lane can make. NHWC gives a pixel's channels locality and lets one load carry a whole pixel when channels are padded to 4; NCHW gives each channel a unit-stride stream. Neither is wrong, and both lose if the kernel accesses one byte at a time.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
md: Best fit plus split plus merge keeps reuse high, but a free hole only helps if it is big enough. Watch the gap between total free and the largest free block, not just the totals.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
md: Count distinct 32-byte sectors per warp request. 4 for 32 consecutive floats is ideal; 32 is the worst case and wastes 87.5% of the traffic.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Reading the Speed Of Light rows
md: Speed Of Light does not tell you what to fix. It tells you which of four investigations to open, and whether the kernel has any headroom at all.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
md: `__syncthreads()` may appear in conditional code only if the condition evaluates the same way for every thread in the block. Otherwise execution may hang or produce unintended side effects. Hoist the barrier out of the branch.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
md: Global search never retrieves by similarity. It asks every community at one level, lets the LLM score how useful each partial answer is, and keeps the best points. That is what makes it work for questions that look like nothing in the corpus.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Group-relative advantages: the baseline from sibling answers
md: In GRPO a sample's advantage means "how much better than its siblings on the same question". If all siblings agree (all right or all wrong), there is nothing to learn from that question.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
md: Prediction at a stop = scheduled instant + the delay from the nearest StopTimeUpdate at or before it, unless that update is NO_DATA. SKIPPED stops are passed through, earlier stops are never filled in, and an absolute time beats a delay.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Kevin Mitnick: social engineering and the longest sentence of its day
md: Social engineering attacks the process, not the person. The fix is a process in which identity is proven through a channel the requester does not control (call-back to a number on file, manager approval, in-person check), and every reset is logged and reviewed.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Target, Sony and OPM: breaches that reached boardrooms and governments
md: Target and OPM both began with a third party's credentials and both had warnings that went unanswered. The lasting changes were about identity: MFA for everyone who logs in remotely, tight scoping of vendor access, and an alert process that someone actually owns.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: A higher IPC is not automatically better. A thread spinning on a lock retires instructions quickly, so it shows high IPC while making no logical progress. Judge IPC together with the instruction count and the run time.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Mitigations, their costs, and checking a real machine
md: `mitigations=off` is sometimes recommended in benchmark blogs. On any machine that runs code you do not fully trust (a browser, CI jobs, containers from others, VMs of other tenants), that trades a few percent of speed for letting that code read memory it should not. Measure your workload first; most of the cost is concentrated in system-call-heavy paths.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: TE.TE and lenient parsing: when headers are spelled oddly
md: A blocklist (for example, refusing requests that contain the word chunked twice) is not a fix. The space of odd spellings is large and each server normalises differently. The fix is a **strict grammar at every hop**: accept only what the RFC allows, reject everything else with 400, and close the connection.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Path confusion at scale: delimiters, studies and ChatGPT 2023
md: Never let the cache infer cacheability from what the URL looks like. Let the origin declare it with Cache-Control, make the cache honour it, and cache by allow-list (a static directory, matching Content-Type) rather than by deny-list.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Do not over-learn the Redis story as "THP copy-on-write always copies 2 MiB". In current `mm/huge_memory.c`, a write to a shared anonymous THP splits the mapping and copies one 4 KiB page. What remains true is that fork-heavy writers churn their huge mappings, and the projects' own guidance (Redis: disable THP; PostgreSQL: THP currently discouraged, explicit huge_pages recommended) is what to follow.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Design rule of thumb from published ablations: keep roughly 8% to 12% of layers as global attention, spread them evenly, start with an SSM layer, and expect long-context KV savings close to (attention layers in the Transformer you replace) / (attention layers you keep), at equal KV heads: 32 / 4 = 8x for Nemotron-H-8B vs Nemotron-T-8B, not 52 / 4 = 13x.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
md: Use HyDE where its strength is real: no labels, a weak or unsupervised encoder, domain or format shift, and a latency budget of seconds. Keep the query in the average, cap passage length, sample in parallel, and route by query type. The paper itself suggests serving HyDE early, then shifting traffic to a supervised retriever as logs grow, keeping HyDE for rare and emerging queries.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
md: Ask two questions of any industrial protocol: does the receiver verify who sent this command, and can it tell if the command was changed or replayed? For classic Modbus and plain DNP3 the answer is no, so the network around them must do that job.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
md: In OT incident response, first make the process safe (using instruments you trust), then keep it running by hand if needed, and only then contain, investigate and restore from offline backups.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Case: ruby-saml CVE-2024-45409 and the GitLab SAML bypass (2024)
md: MFA at the IdP protects the IdP's login. It does nothing for an SP whose verification code can be fooled, because the attacker skips the IdP entirely. Patch SAML libraries as fast as you patch internet-facing servers, and correlate SP logins with IdP sign-ins.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Case: Okta's support system and the stolen HAR files (2023)
md: Session tokens are credentials, wherever they are written down: HAR files, logs, screenshots, crash dumps. Shorten their lives, bind them to the network or device they were issued to, and treat any system that stores them (a support desk included) as part of your identity perimeter.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access: why admin rights differ, and the Snowden case
md: Administrators are trusted to touch everything, so their misuse looks like their job. Detection only works if privileged activity is logged somewhere the administrator cannot edit, and reviewed by someone else (AC-5 and AC-6(9), log the use of privileged functions).

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Rejecting bad matches, warping, and direct ECC alignment
md: Those border zeros look like a dark region in the warped image, and subtracting it from the reference flags a band of fake change along the edges. Warp an all-ones image with the same H to get a validity mask, and ignore pixels outside it.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Preparation: plan, people, contacts, retainers and logs
md: A plan that has never been exercised is a guess. The HSE review recommends testing plans against a catastrophic ransomware scenario in which all IT, all security tools and all usual communication channels are unavailable for weeks.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Building a timeline: super timelines, plaso and a worked merge
md: Never mix time zones silently. Convert everything to UTC at ingestion and keep the original value and its assumed zone, so that a later correction (a server set to the wrong zone, a drifting clock) can be applied and explained.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Heartland and TalkTalk: SQL injection as the way in
md: Both breaches started with a well-known bug class in a web page, and both turned into something much larger: lateral movement into a payment network in one case, and a forgotten set of acquired pages exposing a customer database in the other. You cannot fix pages you do not know you run, so asset inventory is a defence against injection too.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: A classic bug: `char buf[4096];` on the stack of a function that preps a read, submits, and returns. The kernel later writes 4096 bytes into a stack frame that now belongs to someone else. Buffers belong to the kernel from submission until the matching CQE.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Secure boot: a chain of trust that starts in ROM
md: Two classic mistakes. First, checking a hash without a signature: a hash (or CRC) catches corruption but anyone can recompute it for their own image. Second, trusting the public key inside the image without comparing it to the fingerprint in OTP: then any key the attacker generates is "valid". The fingerprint check is what binds the image to the maker.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: One thread for every request: how Node.js runs JavaScript
md: "Async" does not mean "parallel". `async` functions and promises still run their JavaScript on the Event Loop; only waiting (for the network, a file, a timer) happens elsewhere. A slow loop inside an `async` handler blocks every other user exactly like a slow loop anywhere else.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Deserialisation in JavaScript: node-serialize to React2Shell
md: Hosting providers deployed temporary WAF rules, and the React team said plainly: "You should not depend on these to secure your app, and still update immediately." A WAF matches request shapes; the bug was in how valid-looking data was interpreted. Patch the library.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: tcmalloc: rseq per-CPU caches, spans and Temeraire
md: A restartable sequence must tolerate running its prefix many times, so everything before the commit must be side-effect free or harmless to repeat. Writing slot 5 twice is harmless here only because nothing reads beyond `current`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A configuration is only ever best **for a shape on a device**. That is why the tuning result has to be stored under a key that contains the shape, and why `triton.autotune` takes `key=['M', 'N', 'K']`: the docs say a change in those values triggers evaluation of all provided configs.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
md: Scaling rule for bypass stacks: **one queue, one owner**. Hardware queues give each core a private path to the device, mempool caches give it private buffers, and rings or messages are the only places cores meet, always in bursts.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Inside a vulnerable IOCTL handler, and the fix
md: Access control decides *who* may ask; constraints decide *what* can be asked. An admin-only device still makes a perfect BYOVD tool if its handler writes any register or any address. A driver is safe to leave on a machine only when even an administrator cannot use it to do more than its job.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Responding to a BYOVD alert, and the cost of kernel code
md: BYOVD response starts from two assumptions: the attacker is already admin, and the host's sensor may be blind. Contain from outside the host, scope by hash and service name across the fleet, reboot to unload, and fix the gap that let the driver load.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Temperature: amplifying the small probabilities
md: Temperature does not change the argmax, the class with the highest score. Running the deployed student at T greater than 1 does not change its top-1 predictions at all; it only makes its probabilities less confident. Temperature is a training-time device for distillation (and a separate sampling knob for generative models).

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
md: Before writing an LLM distillation loss: confirm a teacher exists or will be reused; use logits when you can, text (Seq-KD, traces) when you cannot; store top-k with a tail bucket or mix in data loss; switch to a sorted-probability loss across tokenizers; and consider starting the student from a pruned teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Bits per number are not the whole cost. Group metadata adds bits (about 1 per number for FP16 scale and zero per 32), and the full-precision residual matters for short sequences.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Choose by failure mode: FP8 for a near-free 2x; per-channel-key, per-token-value low-bit (KIVI, KVQuant) for 4x to 5x if kernels support it; eviction (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV) when context length is the problem and occasional lost tokens are acceptable; query-aware reads (Quest) or head-aware caches (DuoAttention) when they are not.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Capacity offloading: decoding with KV that does not fit in HBM
md: Exactness differs. Reuse offloading and FlexGen without compression are exact: every key and value is used. InfiniGen and ShadowKV *approximate* attention by skipping tokens judged unimportant, so they are judged on accuracy benchmarks as well as speed. The same selection idea also works for KV that stays in HBM (Quest, H2O), to read or keep fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: Happened-before means *information could have flowed* from a to b through process order and messages. It is a partial order: many pairs of events are simply concurrent, and no clock reading can change that.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: MaxSim: each query token finds its best document token
md: Why max and not average? The ColBERT ablation (an experiment that swaps out one component, retrains, and measures what changes) replaced max with average similarity and MRR@10 dropped noticeably. In the toy, the *founded* row of Doc A averages (0.03 + 0.02 + 0.18 + 0.98 + 0.49) / 5 = 0.34, even though the document contains a near-perfect match. Averaging punishes documents for having other content.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: n continuous thoughts cost n sequential forward passes at inference and n + 1 sequential passes per training example, with no tokens emitted for the latent steps.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Choose by what the extra slots carry. Fixed pause or filler embeddings add width within one pass. Coconut's fed-back hidden states and written CoT add serial depth across passes. Recurrent depth adds serial depth inside the network without any extra tokens.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
md: Pick epsilon, get a guarantee. The PGM-index fixes the last-mile search to 2 epsilon + 1 slots per level, uses the fewest segments that can meet that bound, and so its space adapts to how regular the data is.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
md: RankNet does not need graded labels, only a set of preferred pairs. Burges notes the pairs can even be inconsistent, for example from a confused judge who prefers U1 to U2, U2 to U3 and U3 to U1.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add
md: Forgetting to normalize keys is a real bug, not a detail. Take $k_C$ scaled to length 2 and $\beta=1$: the eigenvalue is $1-4=-3$, so a component along that key is multiplied by -3, 9, -27, 81, -243 over five repeated writes.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
md: `chmod 777` is not a fix for "permission denied". It lets every account on the machine, including a compromised web server account, modify the file. If a script run by root is world-writable, any user can make root run their code. Find the account that actually needs access and grant only that.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: regreSSHion: a signal handler race in the SSH server
md: A signal handler can interrupt any line of code, so it must only do async-signal-safe work, and a fix must be guarded by a test or it can quietly disappear in a refactor, as this one did after 14 years.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Automating a benchmark: SCAP, OpenSCAP and ComplianceAsCode
md: Running every generated fix at once on production is the fastest way to lock yourself out: the same playbook also changes PAM lockout rules, SSH ciphers and firewall policy. Generate, read, tailor, and roll out in stages (next lesson).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: When audit falls behind: backlog, lost events and full disks
md: Size the backlog for bursts (8192 is the packaged default on Ubuntu), choose the failure and disk actions deliberately (availability versus completeness), ship records off the host continuously, and alert on lost > 0 and on hosts that go silent.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Kinsing and TeamTNT, cryptominers on exposed Linux hosts
md: "It is only a miner" is the wrong conclusion. The same access that runs XMRig stole cloud credentials and SSH keys in both cases, and TeamTNT reused them to reach new systems. Treat cryptojacking as a full root compromise.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
md: LLM-as-judge for relevance is a measurement instrument. Like any instrument, you calibrate it against a trusted reference (human gold labels) before you read numbers off it.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Pairwise preference, Elo and Bradley-Terry ratings
md: Do not rank by raw win percentage when models faced different opponents: beating weak models inflates it. BT accounts for who played whom. And never report a ranking without intervals; with few votes, neighbouring models are often statistically tied.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: The scheduler's unit of work is a step with a token budget, not a request. Requests enter and leave between steps, and every step is a fresh decision about who gets how many tokens.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
md: Constrained decoding does not make the model understand the format. It removes the illegal choices at each step and lets the model choose among what is left. An FSM state tells you which tokens are legal; a precomputed index makes that lookup cheap.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: Errors are not equal. A **spurious** filter (q6's remote_ok, q7's required javascript) removes good results and the user never sees them. A **missing** filter only returns extra results the user can see and skip. Track precision and recall of slots separately and weight spurious filters as the worse error.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Write the cost model before choosing the method: calls on the critical path, input tokens, output tokens, and model size. Then check quality on your own queries: the cheapest design that holds your NDCG@10 wins.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
md: Routing failures are silent. A wrong answer from the weak model looks like any other answer, and the dashboard shows only that costs went down. Log the routed model with every response (Bedrock returns it), and compare quality by route, not just overall.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
md: A homography is only correct for planar scenes or pure camera rotation. For a general 3D scene seen from two positions, matches satisfy a fundamental or essential matrix instead, and forcing a homography will reject many correct matches.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: EBR is fast because readers only write their own epoch when they pin, but it is not strictly lock-free for memory: Fraser notes that a process that stalls inside a critical region stops the limbo lists (Fraser's name for the per-epoch garbage bags) from ever being reclaimed. Hazard pointers bound the unreclaimed memory (at most NR nodes) at the cost of publishing and re-validating every pointer before use.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The whole course in one line: a log template is the cheapest useful abstraction over log text, and the only one that turns an unbounded stream of unique strings into a small set of countable events. Everything after it, counting, baselining, sequence models, dashboards, inherits both its power and its errors.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Sigma: one rule format, many SIEMs
md: A converted query is only as right as its pipeline's field mapping. If your SIEM stores Sysmon in a different source, or the 4688 field is NewProcessName rather than Image, the query is valid, runs, and silently matches nothing. Always test converted rules against real events from your own environment.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Build it: YaRN tables and a four-host ring in NumPy
md: The paper's YaRN and Hugging Face's YaRN are different functions in the middle pairs. A checkpoint fine-tuned under one and served under the other sees frequencies it was not trained with. When porting a model between frameworks, compare the generated inv_freq tables, not just the config keys.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: Convergence is not automatic. The toy update halves the distance to its fixed point each step (it is **contractive**); a learned block carries no such guarantee. Some loops diverge, and Huginn's analysis (lesson 7) finds tokens whose states orbit or drift instead of settling.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank (the rank of a matrix is how many independent directions its outputs can point in), so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.
